snippet.title: The Only Living Pickpocket: No Permit Risked Subway Filming | Collider BTS
snippet.description:
Filming The Only Living Pickpocket in New York meant taking John Turturro onto real New York City subway trains, shooting without permits, and hoping the police wouldn't shut everything down. But when two officers approached the production, what happened next was pure New York.

John Turturro and writer-director Noah Segan join Collider to discuss the unconventional filming methods behind their 2026 movie, including the challenges and unexpected rewards of shooting in actual New York neighborhoods.

Segan recalls filming incognito on subway trains when two police officers approached the crew. Instead of stopping the production, the officers recognized Turturro and continued on their way. The filmmakers also explain how real New Yorkers became an essential part of the movie's atmosphere, from spontaneous conversations on the street to a memorable encounter with someone who called Turturro a legend.

The conversation also explores the authentic Queens pawn shop that doubled for a Bronx location, the film's five-week shooting schedule, and the collaboration that helped bring Harry's story to life.

Turturro shares why Segan's screenplay resonated with him, particularly its exploration of aging, economic uncertainty, and a changing New York City.

snippet.title: Wildwood Built 130 Sets to Make Its Fantasy Feel Real | Collider Access
snippet.description:
What does it take to build an entire fantasy world by hand? Collider got an exclusive behind-the-scenes look at LAIKA Studios and the incredible sets, puppets, and costumes being created for the upcoming stop-motion animated movie Wildwood.

With around 130 sets designed and a production nearly twice the size of LAIKA's previous biggest film, Wildwood is taking stop-motion animation to another level. But how do you recreate real Portland landmarks in miniature? What goes into making an entire forest by hand? And how do you design costumes for talking animals?

We explore the making of Wildwood with Jacob Tremblay (Curtis Mehlberg), writer Chris Butler, production designer Nelson Lowry, director of rapid prototyping Brian McLean, and costume designer Deborah Cook. From handmade trees and miniature lighting to elaborate character costumes and massive three-story sets, the team walks us through the extraordinary craftsmanship behind LAIKA's latest fantasy adventure.

Plus, Tremblay shares what surprised him most about seeing the puppets in person and why Curtis' journey from nervous kid to unlikely hero is so relatable.

The conversation also explores how Maya's wardrobe and makeup reflect her transformation over a decade, why Morrison embraced a stripped-down filmmaking approach for certain sequences, and how the production developed a close-knit atmosphere.

snippet.title: James McAvoy on How 2,000 Strangers Helped Make California Schemin’
snippet.description:
James McAvoy reveals how he pulled off one of the most ambitious scenes in California Schemin' despite working with a limited budget. Making his feature directorial debut, McAvoy explains how an unforgettable night in Glasgow helped bring the film's climactic concert to life.

In this Collider interview, McAvoy discusses the challenges of directing California Schemin', including how his team organized a real concert to attract 2,000 audience members for a pivotal scene. He recalls how the Glasgow crowd stayed long after the concert ended to help capture the footage, turning a logistical challenge into one of the production's most memorable experiences.

McAvoy also opens up about why this story resonated with his upbringing in Scotland, the importance of representing working-class communities on screen, and the sacrifices people make while pursuing success in the entertainment industry.

From learning how to manage the unexpected demands of directing to drawing inspiration from filmmakers he's worked with throughout his acting career, McAvoy offers a candid look at making his first feature and why finding the right chemistry between his lead actors was essential.

snippet.title: Fire Country: They Burned a Building to Keep Fire Practical | Collider BTS
snippet.description:
The fire scenes in CBS's Fire Country aren't always what they seem. Production designer Anand Ray joins Collider to explain how the series blends practical fire, elaborate set construction, and visual effects to create convincing emergencies without compromising safety.

Ray reveals that the production has sometimes built entire structures specifically to burn them down. But when real flames aren't an option, the team turns to visual effects to enhance practical elements or create fire that couldn't safely be filmed on location.

One of the most surprising challenges? Shooting a series about wildfires when it's pouring rain. Ray explains how the production works around unpredictable weather while making environments appear dry enough to burn.

The conversation also explores the intricate engineering behind Fire Country's rescue sequences, including deliberately unstable floors, custom-built elevator shafts, and large-scale environments designed around specific action beats.

Beyond the destruction, Ray discusses the collaborative process that makes these sequences possible, from early pencil sketches and clay models to construction, location planning, and coordination with directors.

He also reflects on collaborating with James Strong on the pilot and establishing a realistic visual style that continues to shape the series.
For fans curious about how Fire Country is filmed, this behind-the-scenes interview offers a fascinating look at the practical craftsmanship behind the action.

snippet.title: Verity: Dakota Johnson’s Blood Hit Had to Land First Try | Collider BTS
snippet.description:
Anne Hathaway went underwater herself for one of Verity's most haunting sequences, and the filmmakers reveal just how much of the scene was captured practically rather than created with visual effects.

In this exclusive Collider interview, Verity VFX Supervisor Alex Dreiblatt and VFX Producer Sarah McCulley break down the practical effects, visual effects, and production challenges behind the 2026 adaptation of Colleen Hoover's novel.

Hathaway's underwater sequence wasn't created using a dry-for-wet technique. The actress performed the underwater work herself in a pool, allowing the filmmakers to capture the natural movement of her hair and dress. The VFX team then enhanced the environment with atmospheric details to create the finished sequence.

Dreiblatt and McCulley also reveal how Dakota Johnson's bloody New York City scene became an unexpected public spectacle, with real onlookers and social media footage ultimately contributing to the sequence's realism.

The conversation explores the film's isolated house, the painstaking digital replacement of a seemingly ordinary knife, and the seasonal transformations that made winter locations appear to exist across different times of year.

From practical stunts to nearly invisible digital enhancements, the Verity visual effects team explains how the film's most unsettling moments came together.

snippet.title: Pan's Labyrinth: Doug Jones Was Nearly Blind as the Pale Man | Collider BTS
snippet.description:
Was the fantasy world in Pan's Labyrinth real, or was it all in Ofelia's imagination? Doug Jones, Ivana Baquero, and cinematographer Guillermo Navarro revisit Guillermo del Toro's dark fantasy masterpiece, revealing what the director told them about the film's ambiguous ending and how their interpretations have evolved over time.

Jones recalls asking del Toro whether Ofelia was truly the princess of the underworld or whether the fantasy existed only in her mind. The director's answer left room for both interpretations, although he admitted which one he preferred. Baquero explains why believing in Ofelia's journey was essential to her performance and how her relationship with the character has changed since filming.

The conversation also explores the making of the terrifying Pale Man sequence, including Jones' limited visibility beneath the prosthetics, the surprisingly small hallway used for Ofelia's escape, and the practical filmmaking techniques that made the sequence unforgettable.

Navarro discusses the cinematography behind Pan's Labyrinth, the challenges of blending fantasy and reality, and how production limitations forced the crew to create elaborate sequences using lighting, smoke, and practical effects.

Together, the three reflect on del Toro's directing style, the film's visual storytelling, and why its themes continue to resonate.

snippet.title: Below: Josh Hartnett Had to Be Cast Before the Family | Collider BTS
snippet.description:
Below takes a suspense-first approach to horror, drawing inspiration from classic creature features that understood the power of what audiences couldn't see. Executive producer Jessica Rhoades and creator Jesse McKeown reveal how Netflix's series builds dread through atmosphere, carefully timed reveals, and the haunting coastal setting of Newfoundland.

In this Collider interview, Rhoades and McKeown discuss the creative decisions behind Below, including the influence of John Carpenter's The Fog, Larry Cohen's B-movies, and classic horror filmmaking techniques that rely on shadows and misdirection rather than elaborate visual effects.

The filmmakers also explain how Josh Hartnett helped shape Calvin Penney, a reserved father whose emotional complexity remains largely beneath the surface. They reveal why casting the family required finding actors who genuinely looked and felt connected, and how one crucial casting discovery helped bring the characters together.

Plus, Rhoades and McKeown discuss filming on location in Newfoundland, the challenges of shooting on the water, and why the region's folklore, community, and distinctive culture became essential to the series.

From practical filmmaking challenges to the art of building suspense, this behind-the-scenes conversation explores how Below finds its identity in what it chooses not to reveal.

snippet.description:

In this Collider interview, Cho explains why he initially struggled to envision Pastor Hwan. Without a familiar stock character to draw from, he had to trust the filmmaking process and gradually embrace the character’s more theatrical choices.

Cho also discusses Hwan’s belief that his mother’s prayer saved his life in Iraq and how being the recipient of that perceived miracle informs his faith, mission, and morally ambiguous decisions. He then takes us inside his major sequence with Mahershala Ali, including their preparation together, the challenges presented by a mirror-filled room, and their focus on making the fight believable without hurting each other.

The conversation closes with Cho explaining a subtle but important change to the aftermath of the fight. Rather than emotionally connecting face to face, the characters walk shoulder to shoulder — a choice he felt communicated their moment of understanding more effectively.

snippet.title: Harry Potter: How HBO Turns Britain Into One Wizarding World
snippet.description:
Harry Potter’s new HBO series is turning locations scattered across Britain into one continuous Wizarding World. From connected sets at Leavesden to real streets, forests, villages, and coastlines, the production is combining massive builds with practical locations on an ambitious scale.

The Harry Potter series has constructed Diagon Alley, Gringotts, the Leaky Cauldron, and major Hogwarts interiors so characters can physically move between spaces rather than relying entirely on disconnected sets. Outside Leavesden, filming expands across London, Windsor, Hertfordshire, Devon, and Cornwall, with locations standing in for everything from Hogsmeade Station to Hogwarts’ flying fields.

This behind-the-scenes breakdown also explores how the production transformed real locations, why filming outdoors can turn seconds of footage into hours of work, and how Leavesden helps the crew manage the young cast’s limited shooting hours. With a temporary school accommodating around 150 students on a typical day and the lead actors sometimes available for filming for only about 90 minutes, careful planning is essential.

The result is a production designed to make geographically separate locations feel like a single journey through Harry’s world.

snippet.title: Heart of the Beast Used VFX to Hide Dog Changes | Collider BTS
snippet.description:
Brad Pitt wasn’t number one on the call sheet for Heart of the Beast. The dog was.

Visual effects supervisor François Dumoulin breaks down how the 2026 film blended real German Shepherd performances with seamless CGI to create Odin, Brad Pitt’s canine co-star. Four related dogs played the character on set, with hero dog Uber providing the performance and personality that guided the VFX team’s work.

Dumoulin explains how Pitt constantly adapted his performance to what the dogs naturally did, creating spontaneous moments that were preserved through split-screen composites and subtle visual effects. He also reveals that roughly 10–15% of shots involving Odin received some form of VFX work, ranging from altered fur markings and removed tail wags to a CG prosthetic leg, titanium teeth, and complete digital replacements.

The Heart of the Beast VFX breakdown also explores the terrifying digital wolf fight, shooting New Zealand for Alaska, and the increasingly surreal environments inspired by the characters’ trauma. Dumoulin discusses how director David Ayer wanted the animals to feel heightened rather than documentary-real, even drawing inspiration from kabuki theater masks and Andrei Tarkovsky.

snippet.title: The Love Hypothesis: Lili Reinhart's Wig Had to Disappear | Collider BTS
snippet.description:
The Love Hypothesis transformed Lili Reinhart into brunette Olive Smith with a custom wig so convincing that even crew members working inches from the action didn’t realize it wasn’t her real hair.

Hair designer Frederic Belanger breaks down the process behind Reinhart’s Olive Smith look for Prime Video’s The Love Hypothesis, from choosing the exact shade of brunette to collaborating remotely with wig maker Stacey Butterworth. Belanger explains why the production opted against dyeing Reinhart’s naturally blonde hair, the pressure of making the wig completely seamless on camera, and the subtle “ghost hair” added to give it more natural movement in the wind.

He also reveals how Olive’s hairstyles evolve with the story, reflecting everything from the exhaustion of PhD life to dinners with professors. Plus, Belanger discusses developing Tom Bateman’s hair as Adam, balancing his intimidating “Doctor Evil” reputation with a deliberately wilder look.

Go behind the scenes of The Love Hypothesis with Frederic Belanger for a detailed look at the hair design choices that helped bring the characters from Ali Hazelwood’s story to the screen.

snippet.description:
Neil Patrick Harris and director George Jaques break down one of Sunny Dancer’s trickiest emotional scenes, including the running joke that led Harris to ask Jaques to stop calling it the “Oscar scene.”

Harris explains why playing Patrick’s unexpected emotion proved more difficult than a conventional breakdown, while Jaques reveals how rehearsals, camera placement, and carefully limiting takes helped preserve the performance. Their Sunny Dancer behind-the-scenes conversation also offers a revealing look at Jaques’ approach to directing actors.

The pair also discuss the unusually egalitarian atmosphere Jaques created on set. Cast members traveled together, stayed in the same hotel, had equal-size trailers, and were expected to arrive prepared to play as an ensemble. Jaques shares some of the smaller traditions he uses to support actors, from writing letters on their first day to sending encouraging texts after difficult shoots.

For Harris, those choices helped establish a collaborative environment where experience or status didn’t determine how anyone was treated.
